claim: Empathy for pain engages both shared affective responses and self-other distinction.
source: Empathy for pain engages both shared affective responses and self-other distinction.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about empathy.

claim: Observing others in pain engages neural responses aligning with those coding for the affective component of self-experienced pain, with the anterior insula (aIns) and the anterior mid-cingulate cortex (aMCC) being two key areas.
source: Studies using a wide variety of methods convergently have shown that observing others in pain engages neural responses aligning with those coding for the affective component of self-experienced pain, with the anterior insula (aIns) and the anterior mid-cingulate cortex (aMCC) being two key areas in which such an alignment has been detected (Lamm et al., 2011; Rütgen et al., 2015; Jauniaux et al., 2019; Xiong et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2020; Fallon et al., 2020, for meta-analyses).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior meta-analyses and studies.

claim: There is debate on whether activity in aIns and aMCC should be related to the sharing of pain affect or whether it may result from automatic responses to salient perceptual cues.
source: However, there is consistent debate on whether activity observed in these areas should indeed be related to the sharing of pain affect or whether it may not rather result from automatic responses to salient perceptual cues – with pain vividly expressed on the face being one particularly prominent example (Zaki et al., 2016, for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article discussing this debate.

claim: Contextual factors, individuals' appraisals, and attentional processes impact their exact response to the affective states of others.
source: In this respect, contextual factors, individuals' appraisals, and attentional processes would all impact their exact response to the affective states of others (Gu and Han, 2007; Hein and Singer, 2008, for review; Lamm et al., 2010; Forbes and Hamilton, 2020; Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Coll et al., 2017 proposed a framework that individuals who see identical negative facial expressions of others may have different empathic responses due to distinct contextual information.
source: Recently, Coll et al., 2017 have thus proposed a framework that attempts to capture these influences on affect sharing and empathic responses. This model posits that individuals who see identical negative facial expressions of others may have different empathic responses due to distinct contextual information and that this may depend on identification of the underlying affective state displayed by the other.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Coll et al., 2017.

claim: The right supramarginal gyrus (rSMG) has been suggested to act as a major hub selectively engaged in affective self-other distinction.
source: We focused on the right supramarginal gyrus (rSMG), which has been suggested to act as a major hub selectively engaged in affective self-other distinction (Silani et al., 2013; Steinbeis et al., 2015; Hoffmann et al., 2016; Bukowski et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: rSMG is functionally connected with areas associated with affect processing.
source: Though previous studies have indicated that rSMG is functionally connected with areas associated with affect processing (Mars et al., 2012; Bukowski et al., 2020), we lack more nuanced insights into how exactly rSMG interacts with these areas, and thus how it supports accurate empathic responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mars et al., 2012 and Bukowski et al., 2020.

claim: Participants showed higher ratings for the genuine vs. pretended conditions for ratings of painful expressions in others.
source: For ratings of painful expressions in others (Figure 1C, left), there was a main effect of the factor genuineness: participants showed higher ratings for the genuine vs. pretended conditions, Fgenuineness (1, 42) = 8.816, p=0.005, η² = 0.173.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Participants showed higher ratings for the pain vs. no pain conditions for ratings of painful expressions in others.
source: There was also a main effect of pain: participants showed higher ratings for the pain vs. no pain conditions, Fpain (1, 42) = 1718.645, p<0.001, η² = 0.976.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The interaction term for ratings of painful expressions in others was significant and related to higher ratings for the genuine pain compared to the pretended pain condition.
source: The interaction term was significant as well, Finteraction (1, 42) = 7.443, p=0.009, η² = 0.151, and this was related to higher ratings of painful expressions in others for the genuine pain compared to the pretended pain condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Participants showed higher ratings for the genuine vs. pretended conditions for ratings of painful feelings in others.
source: For ratings of painful feelings in others (Figure 1C, middle), there was a main effect of genuineness: participants showed higher ratings for the genuine vs. pretended conditions, Fgenuineness (1, 42) = 770.140, p<0.001, η² = 0.948.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Participants showed higher ratings for the pain vs. no pain conditions for ratings of painful feelings in others.
source: There was also a main effect of pain, as participants showed higher ratings for the pain vs. no pain conditions, Fpain (1, 42) = 1544.762, p<0.001, η² = 0.974.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The interaction for painful feelings ratings was significant and related to higher ratings for the genuine pain compared to the pretended pain condition.
source: The interaction for painful feelings ratings was significant as well, Finteraction (1, 42) = 752.618, p<0.001, η² = 0.947, and this was related to higher ratings of painful feelings in others for the genuine pain compared to the pretended pain condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Participants showed higher ratings for the genuine vs. pretended conditions for ratings of unpleasantness in self.
source: For ratings of unpleasantness in self (Figure 1C, right), there was a main effect of genuineness: participants showed higher ratings for the genuine vs. pretended conditions, Fgenuineness (1, 42) = 74.989, p<0.001, η² = 0.641.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Participants showed higher ratings for the pain vs. no pain conditions for ratings of unpleasantness in self.
source: There was also a main effect of pain: participants showed higher ratings for the pain vs. no pain conditions, Fpain (1,42) = 254.709, p<0.001, η² = 0.858.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The interaction for unpleasantness ratings was significant and related to higher ratings for the genuine pain compared to the pretended pain condition.
source: The interaction for unpleasantness ratings was significant as well, Finteraction (1, 42) = 73.620, p<0.001, η² = 0.637, and this was related to higher ratings of unpleasantness in self for the genuine pain compared to the pretended pain condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: There was a significant correlation between behavioral ratings of painful feelings in others and unpleasantness in self in the genuine pain condition.
source: We also found a significant correlation between behavioral ratings of painful feelings in others and unpleasantness in self in the genuine pain condition, r = 0.691, p<0.001, while in the pretended pain condition, the correlation was not significant, r = 0.249, p=0.107 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of behavioral data and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The correlation between painful feelings in others and unpleasantness in self was not significant in the pretended pain condition.
source: We also found a significant correlation between behavioral ratings of painful feelings in others and unpleasantness in self in the genuine pain condition, r = 0.691, p<0.001, while in the pretended pain condition, the correlation was not significant, r = 0.249, p=0.107 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of behavioral data and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A bootstrapping comparison showed a significant difference between the two correlation coefficients for genuine pain and pretended pain conditions.
source: A bootstrapping comparison showed a significant difference between the two correlation coefficients, p=0.002, 95 % Confidence Interval (CI) = [0.230, 1.060].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using bootstrapping.

claim: Activations were found in bilateral aIns, aMCC, and rSMG across all three contrasts.
source: Across all three contrasts, we found activations as hypothesized in bilateral aIns, aMCC, and rSMG (Figure 2A and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: Multiple regression analysis demonstrated significant clusters in the left and right anterior insular cortex that were positively correlated with the ratings of unpleasantness in self comparing genuine pain vs. pretended pain.
source: The multiple regression analysis demonstrated significant clusters in the left (peak: [–42, 15,–2]) and right anterior insular cortex (peak: [45, 5, 8]) that were positively correlated with the ratings of unpleasantness in self comparing genuine pain vs. pretended pain.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple regression analysis of fMRI data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There were strong evidence of inhibitory effects on the aIns to rSMG connection both in the genuine pain condition and in the pretended pain condition.
source: We found strong evidence of inhibitory effects on the aIns to rSMG connection both in the genuine pain condition and in the pretended pain condition (Figure 1A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by DCM analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Comparing the strength of modulatory effects on the aIns to rSMG connection revealed a reduced inhibitory effect for genuine pain as opposed to pretended pain.
source: Comparing the strength of these modulatory effects on the aIns to rSMG connection revealed a reduced inhibitory effect for genuine pain as opposed to pretended pain, t41 = 2.671, p=0.011 (meangenuine pain = −0.821, 95% CI = [−0.878, −0.712]; meanpretended pain = −0.934, 95% CI = [−1.076, −0.822]; Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by DCM analysis and statistical comparison shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was no evidence of a modulatory effect on the rSMG to aIns connection.
source: There was no evidence of a modulatory effect on the rSMG to aIns connection.
evidence: This claim is supported by DCM analysis of fMRI data.

claim: For the genuine pain condition, the modulatory effect was significantly related to the rating of painful feelings in others.
source: For the genuine pain condition, we find that the modulatory effect was significantly related to the rating of painful feelings in others (t = 2.317, p=0.026), but not related to the rating of either painful expressions in others (t = −1.492, p=0.144) or unpleasantness in self (t = 0.058, p=0.954).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple linear regression analysis of DCM parameters and behavioral ratings.

claim: For the genuine pain condition, the modulatory effect was not related to the rating of painful expressions in others or unpleasantness in self.
source: For the genuine pain condition, we find that the modulatory effect was significantly related to the rating of painful feelings in others (t = 2.317, p=0.026), but not related to the rating of either painful expressions in others (t = −1.492, p=0.144) or unpleasantness in self (t = 0.058, p=0.954).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple linear regression analysis of DCM parameters and behavioral ratings.

claim: For the pretended pain condition, none of the ratings was significantly related to the modulatory effect.
source: For the pretended pain condition, none of the ratings was significantly related to the modulatory effect (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple linear regression analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the genuine pain condition, the modulatory effect was significantly explained by scores of affective ability and affective reactivity of the ECQ.
source: In the genuine pain condition, we found that the modulatory effect was significantly explained by scores of two subscales, that is affective ability and affective reactivity of the ECQ: Fmodel (1, 39) = 6.829, p=0.003, R2 = 0.270; Baffective ability = 0.052, beta = 0.497, p=0.002; Baffective reactivity = −0.040, beta = −0.421, p=0.008.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple stepwise linear regression analysis of DCM parameters and questionnaire scores.

claim: In the pretended pain condition, none of the three questionnaires significantly predicted variations of the modulatory effect.
source: In the pretended pain condition, none of the three questionnaires significantly predicted variations of the modulatory effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple stepwise linear regression analysis of DCM parameters and questionnaire scores.

claim: The increased activity in aIns for genuine pain as opposed to pretended pain properly reflects affect sharing.
source: The mass-univariate analyses suggest that the increased activity in aIns for genuine pain as opposed to pretended pain properly reflects affect sharing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI data analysis results.

claim: The increased activation in aIns was selectively correlated with ratings of self-oriented unpleasantness and was not correlated with either other-related painful expressions or painful feelings in terms of the regression analysis.
source: However, when comparing genuine pain versus pretended pain, activity in these areas was not only found to be stronger in response to genuine pain, but the increased activation in aIns was also selectively correlated with ratings of self-oriented unpleasantness and was not correlated with either other-related painful expressions or painful feelings in terms of the regression analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis of fMRI data and behavioral ratings.

claim: aIns is more specifically associated with affective representations, while the role of aMCC rather seems to evaluate and regulate emotions that arise due to empathy.
source: That only aIns and not also aMCC shows such correlation may be explained by previous studies, according to which aIns is more specifically associated with affective representations, while the role of aMCC rather seems to evaluate and regulate emotions that arise due to empathy (Fan et al., 2011; Lamm et al., 2011; Jauniaux et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Responses in aIns and aMCC are not simply automatic responses triggered by perceptually salient events but seem to track the actual affective states of the other person.
source: Taken together, the activation and brain-behavior findings provide evidence that responses in aIns (and to a lesser extent also the aMCC) are not simply automatic responses triggered by perceptually salient events (otherwise the increased aIns activation should also be explained by other behavioral ratings in the sense of shared influence by domain-general effects). Rather, they seem to track the actual affective states of the other person, and thus the shared neural representation of that response (see Zhou et al., 2020, for similar recent conclusions based on multi-voxel pattern analyses).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data analysis results, supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2020.

claim: The findings are in line with the proposed model of Coll et al., 2017, which suggests that affect sharing is the consequence of emotion identification.
source: Our findings are also in line with the proposed model of Coll et al., 2017, which suggests that affect sharing is the consequence of emotion identification.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to a cited theoretical model.

claim: Part of the activation in the aIns and aMCC is related to an automatic response, and the added engagement of these areas once they have identified the pain as genuine shows that only in this condition, they then also engage in proper affect sharing.
source: More specifically, while part of the activation in the aIns and aMCC is indeed related to an (presumably earlier) automatic response, the added engagement of these areas once they have identified the pain as genuine shows that only in this condition, they then also engage in proper affect sharing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data analysis results.

claim: The inferior parietal lobule was shown to be generally engaged in selective attention, action observation, and imitating emotions.
source: The inferior parietal lobule was shown to be generally engaged in selective attention, action observation, and imitating emotions (Bach et al., 2010; Pokorny et al., 2015; Gola, 2017; Hawco et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The rSMG allows for a rapid switching between or the integration of self- and other-related representations, as two processes that may underpin the functional basis of successful self-other distinction.
source: Based on such findings, it has been proposed that the rSMG allows for a rapid switching between or the integration of self- and other-related representations, as two processes that may underpin the functional basis of successful self-other distinction (Lamm et al., 2016, for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Theoretical models of empathy suggest that regulation is especially important to avoid empathic over-arousal, which would shift the focus away from empathy and the other's needs, toward taking care of one's own personal distress.
source: Theoretical models of empathy and related socio-affective responses suggest that such regulation is especially important to avoid so-called empathic over-arousal, which would shift the focus away from empathy and the other's needs, toward taking care of one's own personal distress (Batson et al., 1987, for review; Decety and Lamm, 2011, for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The higher rSMG engagement in the genuine pain condition reflects an increasing demand for self-other distinction imposed by the stronger shared negative affect experienced in this condition.
source: Concerning the current findings, we thus propose that the higher rSMG engagement in the genuine pain condition reflects an increasing demand for self-other distinction imposed by the stronger shared negative affect experienced in this condition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI data analysis results.

claim: Areas such as the aIns and rSMG may play a key role in comparing self-related information with the sensory evidence.
source: Various theoretical accounts suggest that areas such as the aIns and rSMG may play a key role in comparing self-related information with the sensory evidence (Decety and Lamm, 2007, for review; Seth, 2013, for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: According to theories on predictive processing and active inference, the brain can be regarded as a 'prediction machine', in which the top-down signals pass over predictions and the bottom-up signals convey prediction errors across different levels of cortical hierarchies.
source: According to recent theories on predictive processing (Clark, 2013, for review) and active inference (Friston, 2010, for review), the brain can be regarded as a "prediction machine", in which the top-down signals pass over predictions and the bottom-up signals convey prediction errors across different levels of cortical hierarchies (Chen et al., 2009; Friston, 2010, for review; Bastos et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles and research papers.

claim: Top-down predictions are mediated by inhibitory neural connections.
source: It is suggested that these top-down predictions are mediated by inhibitory neural connections (Zhang et al., 2008; Bastos et al., 2015; Miska et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The inhibitory connection from aIns to rSMG can be explained as the predictive mismatch between the top-down predictions of self-related information and sensory inputs.
source: Our findings align with such views, by suggesting that the inhibitory connection from aIns to rSMG can be explained as the predictive mismatch between the top-down predictions of self-related information (e.g., personal affect) and sensory inputs (e.g., pain facial expressions).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DCM analysis results in the context of predictive processing theories.

claim: The suppression of neural activity leads to an explaining away of incoming bottom-up prediction error.
source: This suppression of neural activity leads to an explaining away of incoming bottom-up prediction error.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on predictive processing theory.

claim: The absence of any condition-dependent modulatory effects on the rSMG to aIns connection suggests that the influence of the task conditions is sufficiently modeled by the predictions from aIns to rSMG.
source: This is reflected by the absence of any condition-dependent modulatory effects on the rSMG to aIns connection, suggesting that the influence of the task conditions is sufficiently modeled by the predictions from aIns to rSMG.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DCM analysis results.

claim: The stronger inhibition for pretended pain, compared to genuine pain, could indicate a higher demand to overcome the mismatch between the visual inputs and the agent's prior beliefs and contextual information about the situation.
source: Therefore, the stronger inhibition for pretended pain, compared to genuine pain, could indicate a higher demand to overcome the mismatch between the visual inputs and the agent's prior beliefs and contextual information about the situation (i.e., "this person looks like in pain, but I know he/she does not actually feel it").
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DCM analysis results.

claim: A dynamic interaction between sensory-driven and control processes is underlying the modulatory effect.
source: We speculate that a dynamic interaction between sensory-driven and control processes is underlying the modulatory effect: when individuals realized after an initial sensory-driven response to the facial expression that it was not genuinely expressing pain, control, and appraisal processes led to a reappraisal of the triggered emotional response, and thus a dampening of the unpleasantness.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The reduced inhibition in the genuine pain condition could be a mechanism that explains the higher rSMG activation in this condition.
source: The reduced inhibition in the genuine pain condition could moreover be a mechanism that explains the higher rSMG activation in this condition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DCM and fMRI analysis results.

claim: The modulation of aIns to rSMG is implicated in encoding others' emotional states, which serves as a functional foundation for self-other processing when participants engaged in genuine affect sharing.
source: We deem it more plausible, though, that the correlation findings provide further evidence that the modulation of aIns to rSMG is implicated in encoding others' emotional states, which serves as a functional foundation for self-other processing when participants engaged in genuine affect sharing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation findings between DCM parameters and behavioral ratings.

claim: The found correlation relates to cognitive evaluations of the other's pain rather than to own affect, as tracked by the unpleasantness in self-ratings.
source: It is also interesting to note that the found correlation relates to cognitive evaluations of the other's pain rather than to own affect, as tracked by the unpleasantness in self-ratings.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation findings.

claim: Kanske et al., 2016 found that the inhibition of the temporoparietal junction (TPJ) by the aIns was linked to interactions between Theory of Mind (ToM) and empathic distress.
source: This would to some extent be in line with DCM findings by Kanske et al., 2016. These authors found that the inhibition of the temporoparietal junction (TPJ) by the aIns was linked to interactions between Theory of Mind (ToM) and empathic distress, that is the interaction of 'cognitive' vs. 'affective' processes engaged in understanding others' cognitive and affective states.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kanske et al., 2016.

claim: The right TPJ is an overarching area involved in self-other distinction of which rSMG is considered a part or at least closely connected to.
source: Note that the right TPJ is an overarching area involved in self-other distinction of which rSMG is considered a part or at least closely connected to Decety and Lamm, 2007, for review.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: When participants shared genuine affect, the inhibitory effect on the aIns to rSMG connection was positively correlated with affective ability and negatively correlated with affective reactivity.
source: When participants shared genuine affect, the inhibitory effect on the aIns to rSMG connection was positively correlated with affective ability and negatively correlated with affective reactivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis of DCM parameters and questionnaire scores.

claim: Affective ability reflects the capacity to subjectively share emotions with others, while affective reactivity plays a role in the susceptibility to vicarious distress and thus to more automatic responses to another's emotion.
source: Affective ability reflects the capacity to subjectively share emotions with others, while affective reactivity plays a role in the susceptibility to vicarious distress and thus to more automatic responses to another's emotion (Batchelder et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Batchelder et al., 2017.

claim: In the genuine pain condition, which requires an accurate sharing of pain, rSMG interacts with aIns to achieve 'affective-to-affective' self-other distinction.
source: Taken together, the DCM results and their qualification by the correlation findings suggest that in the genuine pain condition, which requires an accurate sharing of pain, rSMG interacts with aIns to achieve 'affective-to-affective' self-other distinction – that is disambiguating affective signals originating in the self from those attributable to the other person.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DCM and correlation analysis results.

claim: The aIns to rSMG connection in the pretended pain condition may reflect 'cognitive-to-affective' self-other distinction, which helps resolve conflicting information between the top-down contextual information and what seems an unavoidable affective response to the highly salient perceptual cue of the facial expression of pain.
source: The aIns to rSMG connection in the pretended pain condition may reflect a related, yet slightly distinct mechanism. Here, it seems that 'cognitive-to-affective' self-other distinction is at play, which helps resolve conflicting information between the top-down contextual information (i.e., that the demonstrator is not actually in pain) from what seems an unavoidable affective response to the highly salient perceptual cue of the facial expression of pain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DCM analysis results.

claim: This inhibitory effect might be related to socioemotional disturbances of individuals with autism spectrum disorders (ASD), who show impairments in social cognition, including self- and other-related processing.
source: This inhibitory effect might be related to socioemotional disturbances of individuals with autism spectrum disorders (ASD), who show impairments in social cognition, including self- and other-related processing (Hoffmann et al., 2016; Lamm et al., 2016, for review).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ASD individuals likely exhibit distinct inhibition of the aIns-to-rSMG connectivity pattern compared to healthy controls.
source: It is thus likely that ASD individuals exhibit distinct inhibition of the aIns-to-rSMG connectivity pattern compared to healthy controls.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings and prior research on ASD.

claim: The enhanced aIns activation in the genuine pain condition mainly tracked personal unpleasantness rather than perceptually domain-general processes.
source: As we found the enhanced aIns activation in the genuine pain condition mainly tracked personal unpleasantness rather than perceptually domain-general processes, and because the effect size of the pain expression difference was much smaller than for the affect ratings, we consider this difference did not fundamentally influence the interpretation of our findings.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regression analysis results.

claim: The study design did not aim to explicitly quantify self-other distinction.
source: An additional limitation was that our study design did not aim to explicitly quantify self-other distinction. Rather, in line with previous research and based on our theoretical framework and rationale, we inferred the engagement of this process from the experimental conditions and the associated behavioral and neural responses.
evidence: This is a statement about the study design and methodology.

claim: The study provides evidence that empathy-related responses in the aIns can indeed be linked to affective sharing, rather than attributing them to responses triggered only by perceptual saliency.
source: In conclusion, the current study advances our understanding of two main aspects of empathy. First, we provide evidence that empathy-related responses in the aIns can indeed be linked to affective sharing, rather than attributing them to responses triggered only by perceptual saliency.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data analysis results.

claim: The study shows how aIns and rSMG are orchestrated to track what another person really feels, thus enabling us to appropriately respond to their actual needs.
source: Second, we show how aIns and rSMG are orchestrated to track what another person really feels, thus enabling us to appropriately respond to their actual needs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the DCM analysis results.

claim: Forty-three participants (21 females; age: Mean = 26.72 years, S.D. = 4.47) were entered into analyses.
source: Data of the remaining 43 participants (21 females; age: Mean = 26.72 years, S.D. = 4.47) were entered into analyses.
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: Five participants were excluded because of excessive head motion.
source: Five of them were excluded because of excessive head motion ( >15% scans with the frame-wise displacement over 0.5 mm in one session).
evidence: This is a description of the exclusion criteria applied to the data.

claim: The minimum sample size statistically required for this study was 34.
source: After calculation, the minimum sample size statistically required for this study was 34 (α = 0.05, two-tailed, 1−β = 0.80).
evidence: This is a result of a priori power analysis.

claim: All participants were right-handed.
source: All participants were being right-handed (self-reported) and provided written consent including post-disclosure of any potential deception.
evidence: This is a description of the participant characteristics.

claim: The study was approved by the ethics committee of the Medical University of Vienna.
source: The study was approved by the ethics committee of the Medical University of Vienna and was conducted in line with the latest version of the World Medical Association, 2013.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: All painful expressions were acted, as the needle was a telescopic needle.
source: Unbeknownst to the participants, all painful expressions were acted, as the needle was a telescopic needle (i.e., a needle that seemed to enter the cheek upon contact, but in reality, was invisibly retracting into the syringe).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental manipulation.

claim: An online validation study with N = 110 participants was performed to validate the stimuli.
source: To validate the stimuli, we performed an online validation study with N = 110 participants, who were asked to rate a total of 120 video clips of 2 s duration of the two conditions (60 of each condition) showing painful expressions (i.e., the genuine and the pretended pain conditions).
evidence: This is a description of the validation study methodology.

claim: Survey data of 62 of 110 participants were entered into analysis for the validation study.
source: Survey data of 62 of 110 participants (34 females; age: mean = 28.71 years, S.D. = 10.11) were entered into analysis (inclusion criteria: false rate for the test questions < 2/8, survey duration > 20 min and <150 min, and the maximum number of continuous identical ratings < 5).
evidence: This is a description of the validation study sample and inclusion criteria.

claim: Videos of six demonstrators were excluded for which participants showed a significant difference in painful expressions in others between the genuine pain and the pretended pain conditions.
source: Based on this validation step, we had to exclude videos of six demonstrators (three females) for which participants showed a significant difference in painful expressions in others between the genuine pain and the pretended pain conditions.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus selection process based on validation data.

claim: Videos of 14 demonstrators were selected for the subsequent pilot study.
source: As a result of this validation, videos of 14 demonstrators (7 females), which showed no difference in the pain expression rating between genuine and pretended conditions and which overall showed comparable mean ratings in all three ratings, were selected for the subsequent pilot study.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus selection process.

claim: In the pilot study, 47 participants were recruited for a behavioral experiment in the behavioral laboratory.
source: In the pilot study, 47 participants (24 females; age: mean = 26.28 years, S.D. = 8.80) were recruited for a behavioral experiment in the behavioral laboratory.
evidence: This is a description of the pilot study sample.

claim: Videos of two demonstrators were excluded after the pilot study for whom the pain expression rating difference between the pretended vs. genuine expressions was large.
source: Upon screening for video clips that showed aberrant responses, we excluded videos of two demonstrators (one female), for whom the pain expression rating difference between the pretended vs. genuine expressions was large.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus selection process based on pilot data.

claim: Forty-eight videos of 12 demonstrators entered the analyses for the pilot study.
source: Forty-eight videos of 12 demonstrators entered the following analyses.
evidence: This is a description of the final stimulus set for the pilot study.

claim: In the pilot study, the main effect of genuineness was not significant and low in effect size for painful expressions in others.
source: For the main effect of genuineness (genuine vs. pretended), it was not significant and low in effect size for painful expressions in others (Fgenuineness (1, 46) = 2.939, p=0.093, η² = 0.060), but was significant with high effect size for the painful feelings in others (Fgenuineness (1, 46) = 280.112, p<0.001, η² = 0.859) as well as the unpleasantness in self (Fgenuineness (1, 46) = 43.143, p<0.001, η² = 0.484).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of pilot study data.

claim: In the pilot study, the main effect of genuineness was significant with high effect size for the painful feelings in others and the unpleasantness in self.
source: For the main effect of genuineness (genuine vs. pretended), it was not significant and low in effect size for painful expressions in others (Fgenuineness (1, 46) = 2.939, p=0.093, η² = 0.060), but was significant with high effect size for the painful feelings in others (Fgenuineness (1, 46) = 280.112, p<0.001, η² = 0.859) as well as the unpleasantness in self (Fgenuineness (1, 46) = 43.143, p<0.001, η² = 0.484).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of pilot study data.

claim: In the pilot study, the main effects of pain for all three questions were found significant with high effect size.
source: The main effects of pain (pain vs. no pain) for all three questions were found significant with high effect size (the smallest effect size was for the rating of unpleasantness in self, Fpain (1, 46) = 82.199, p<0.001, η² = 0.641).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of pilot study data.

claim: Participants rated the painfulness of the demonstrators to be substantially higher when it was genuine as compared to those that were pretended in the pilot study.
source: More specifically, as expected and required for the main study, participants rated the painfulness of the demonstrators to be substantially higher when it was genuine as compared to those that were pretended, and this also resulted in much higher unpleasantness experienced in the self.
evidence: This is a summary of the pilot study findings.

claim: The two conditions did not differ with respect to the ratings of the painful facial expressions in the pilot study.
source: It is worth noting that, the two conditions did not differ with respect to the ratings of the painful facial expressions, implying that putative differences in ratings as well as the subsequent brain imaging data could only be attributed to the contextual appraisal of the demonstrators' actual painful states, rather than the differences in facial pain perception.
evidence: This is a summary of the pilot study findings.

claim: Videos of 12 demonstrators (6 females) were used in the main fMRI experiment.
source: Based on this pilot study, we thus decided on video clips of 12 demonstrators (6 females) in the main fMRI experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the final stimulus set for the main experiment.

claim: The experiment was implemented using Cogent 2000 (version 1.33).
source: The experiment was implemented using Cogent 2000 (version 1.33; http://www.vislab.ucl.ac.uk/cogent_2000.php).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental software.

claim: Participants were explicitly instructed to recreate the feelings of the demonstrators shown in the videos as vividly and intensely as possible.
source: Participants were explicitly instructed to recreate the feelings of the demonstrators shown in the videos as vividly and intensely as possible.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental instructions.

claim: The demonstrators appearing in the genuine and pretended conditions were counterbalanced across participants.
source: We also counterbalanced the demonstrators appearing in the genuine and pretended conditions across participants, thus controlling for differences in behavioral and brain response that could be explained by differences between the stimulus sets.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The participant performed the fMRI experiment in two runs.
source: The participant performed the fMRI experiment in two runs (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure shown in Figure 1.

claim: Each run was composed of two blocks showing genuine pain and two blocks showing pretended pain.
source: Each run was composed of two blocks showing genuine pain and two blocks showing pretended pain.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In each block, the participant watched nine video clips containing both painful and neutral videos.
source: In each block, the participant watched nine video clips containing both painful and neutral videos.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: fMRI data were collected using a Siemens Magnetom Skyra MRI scanner with a 32-channel head coil.
source: fMRI data were collected using a Siemens Magnetom Skyra MRI scanner (Siemens, Erlangen, Germany), with a 32-channel head coil.
evidence: This is a description of the MRI equipment.

claim: Functional whole-brain scans were collected using a multiband-accelerated T2*-weighted echoplanar imaging sequence.
source: Functional whole-brain scans were collected using a multiband-accelerated T2*-weighted echoplanar imaging sequence (multiband acceleration factor = 4, interleaved ascending acquisition in multi-slice mode, 52 slices co-planar to the connecting line between anterior and posterior commissure, TR = 1200 ms, TE = 34 ms, acquisition matrix = 96 × 96 voxels, FOV = 210 × 210 mm2, flip angle = 66°, inter-slice gap = 0.4 mm, voxel size = 2.2 × 2.2 × 2 mm3).
evidence: This is a description of the MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Two functional imaging runs, each lasting around 16 min, were performed.
source: Two functional imaging runs, each lasting around 16 min (~800 images per run), were performed.
evidence: This is a description of the MRI acquisition.

claim: Imaging data were preprocessed with a combination of Nipype and MATLAB, with Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM12).
source: Imaging data were preprocessed with a combination of Nipype (Gorgolewski et al., 2011) and MATLAB (version R2018b 9.5.0; MathWorks), with Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM12; https://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/software/spm12/).
evidence: This is a description of the data preprocessing software.

claim: Data scrubbing of the functional scans was performed for those whose frame-wise displacements (FD) were over 0.5 mm.
source: To improve data quality, we performed data scrubbing of the functional scans for those whose frame-wise displacements (FD) were over 0.5 mm (Power et al., 2012; Power et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the data quality control procedure, supported by citations.

claim: An initial threshold of p<0.001 (uncorrected) at the voxel level and a family-wise error (FWE) correction (p<0.05) at the cluster level were applied.
source: We applied an initial threshold of p<0.001 (uncorrected) at the voxel level and a family-wise error (FWE) correction (p<0.05) at the cluster level.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical thresholding procedure.

claim: Dynamic causal modeling (DCM) was used to estimate the effective connectivity between the ROIs based on the tasked-related brain responses.
source: To investigate the functional network involved in affective processes and self-other distinction and how it was modulated by our experimental manipulations (i.e., genuine pain and pretended pain), we used DCM to estimate the effective connectivity between the ROIs based on the tasked-related brain responses (Stephan and Friston, 2010, for review).
evidence: This is a description of the DCM analysis method, supported by a citation.

claim: The DCM analyses were conducted with DCM12.5 implemented in SPM12 (v. 7771).
source: The DCM analyses were conducted with DCM12.5 implemented in SPM12 (v. 7771).
evidence: This is a description of the DCM analysis software.

claim: One participant was excluded from DCM analysis as no voxels survived significance testing.
source: One participant was excluded as no voxels survived significance testing.
evidence: This is a description of the exclusion criteria for DCM analysis.

claim: Group-level DCM inference was performed using parametric empirical Bayes.
source: Finally, group-level DCM inference was performed using parametric empirical Bayes (Zeidman et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is a description of the DCM analysis method, supported by a citation.

claim: An automatic search over the entire model space (max. n = 256) was conducted using Bayesian model reduction and random-effects Bayesian model averaging.
source: We conducted an automatic search over the entire model space (max. n = 256) using Bayesian model reduction and random-effects Bayesian model averaging, resulting in a final group model that takes accuracy, complexity, and uncertainty into account (Zeidman et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is a description of the DCM model selection procedure, supported by a citation.

claim: The threshold of the Bayesian posterior probability was set to pp>0.95 (i.e., strong evidence).
source: The threshold of the Bayesian posterior probability was set to pp>0.95 (i.e., strong evidence) but we reported all parameters above pp>0.75 (i.e., positive evidence) for full transparency of the DCM results.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical threshold for DCM analysis.

claim: The model without any interaction outperformed other models for both genuine pain and pretend pain in the regression analysis of DCM parameters with behavioral ratings.
source: Considering that interactions between behavioral ratings might contribute to the regression model, we tested five regression models (with and without interaction; See Supplementary file 1) for both genuine pain and pretended pain. Results showed that for both genuine pain and pretend pain, the model without any interaction outperformed other models.
evidence: This claim is supported by model comparison analysis.

claim: Two participants did not complete all three questionnaires and were excluded from the regression analyses with questionnaires.
source: As two participants did not complete all three questionnaires, we excluded their data from the regression analyses.
evidence: This is a description of the exclusion criteria for regression analysis.

claim: A conservative threshold of VIF < 5 was used as a sign of no severe multicollinearity.
source: Here we used a rather conservative threshold of VIF < 5 as a sign of no severe multicollinearity (Menard, 2002; James et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the multicollinearity diagnostic threshold, supported by citations.
